passage: I teach in the corridor beside Lakshmi's classroom, and through the open door I saw the reading circle. Lakshmi, five, sat with her shoulders high and tight, near her ears, while the teacher Sangeeta asked who would like to tell the class about the puppy. Lakshmi's hand went halfway up, then down. Sangeeta smiled and nodded at her and took a slow breath, exaggerated, and Lakshmi copied it. Her shoulders dropped, and she started, "My puppy has a white paw."

qa.q: What did Lakshmi say about her puppy?
qa.a: She said, "My puppy has a white paw."

qa.q: What do Lakshmi's high shoulders and half-raised hand suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she was nervous about speaking, though she also wanted to share. She might simply have been cold.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi speak?
qa.a: Sangeeta gave a friendly nod and modelled a slow breath, which Lakshmi copied.

qa.q: How does the observer in the corridor see the moment differently from Lakshmi?
qa.a: The observer sees her body and Sangeeta's calm nod but can only guess at Lakshmi's feelings.

grounding: A child's tense shoulders before speaking show nervousness, and slow breaths and a friendly nod from the teacher help.

passage:
Day one: in the Halifax classroom, Elizabeth, five, kept her shoulders stiff and her mouth shut while Ms Anjali asked for show-and-tell. Anjali smiled and moved on.
Day three: Elizabeth's shoulders rose again as she stood to speak. Anjali gave her a small nod. Elizabeth breathed out and said one sentence about her shell.
Day six: her shoulders were only slightly tight; she took a slow breath and showed the whole class, adding, "I got it at the beach."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth show the class on day six?
qa.a: She showed her shell and told the class, "I got it at the beach."

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's change in shoulders across the days suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: They suggest her nervousness eased as she got used to speaking, and Anjali's nod probably helped. She may still feel some nerves, since her shoulders were slightly tight on day six.

qa.q: What could Anjali keep doing to help Elizabeth?
qa.a: She can keep the friendly nod and remind Elizabeth to take a slow breath before she speaks, without pushing her.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel on day six after she finishes speaking?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and pleased that she managed, and more ready to try again.

grounding: Tense shoulders before speaking show nervousness that eases with slow breaths and a friendly nod.

passage: Show-and-tell day, and the rain was roaring on the school's tin roof. Pooja stood at the front holding her shell, her shoulders pulled up almost to her ears. She opened her mouth and nothing came out. Parul Ma'am caught her eye across the room and gave a slow, friendly nod. Then she put a hand on her own tummy and breathed out, big and slow. Pooja copied. Her shoulders slid down. “This shell,” she said, loud enough over the rain, “is from the sea.”

qa.q: What was Pooja holding for show-and-tell?
qa.a: Her shell.

qa.q: What do Pooja's raised shoulders suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she was nervous about speaking in front of the class, made harder by the loud rain. She may also have worried that no one would hear her.

qa.q: What did Parul Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She gave a slow, friendly nod and modelled a big, slow breath, which Pooja copied until her shoulders relaxed.

qa.q: How might the class have seen Pooja's first silence?
qa.a: Some might think she forgot or didn't want to speak, not realising she was nervous and tense.

grounding: A child's tight shoulders before speaking in class show nervousness, and slow breaths and the teacher's nod help.

passage: At the Monday assembly in the city school, it was Farhan's turn to say “Good morning” into the microphone. He walked up with his shoulders stiff and high, arms straight down. Mehak Ma'am stood beside the stage. She bent down and whispered, “Shoulders down like a sleepy cat. One big breath.” Farhan lifted and dropped his shoulders, breathed, and she nodded at him. “Good… morning, everyone!” His voice wobbled but carried. The whole school said it back, and he grinned all the way to his line.

qa.q: What was Farhan's job at the assembly?
qa.a: To say “Good morning” into the microphone.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling as he walked up with stiff, high shoulders?
qa.a: He was nervous about speaking in front of the whole school. He may also have felt excited, since he grinned afterwards.

qa.q: What would you advise a teacher helping a nervous child at assembly?
qa.a: Give one simple, playful body cue like dropping the shoulders and a breath, then a friendly nod before the child speaks.

qa.q: What was it like for Farhan when the whole school said it back?
qa.a: It likely felt like relief and pride, turning his nerves into a big grin.

grounding: A child tenses his shoulders before speaking at assembly, and a teacher's breathing cue and nod help him relax.

passage:
“Say it to me first,” said Binita, sitting on the bed. “Pretend I'm Miss.”
Ujjwal stood up. His shoulders crept up toward his ears. “Miss… can I… be the…”
“Stop. Look at your shoulders.”
Ujjwal looked. “They're up.”
“Drop them. Breathe out like blowing a candle.”
He blew. His shoulders fell. “Miss, can I be the lion in the play?”
“Perfect,” said Binita. The next morning, before class, Ujjwal whispered to her, “Shoulders.” She blew a pretend candle, and he went in.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal want to be in the play?
qa.a: The lion.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when his shoulders crept up?
qa.a: He was nervous about asking his teacher, and wanted the part badly. He may also have felt shy even in front of his sister.

qa.q: Which step worked, and why?
qa.a: Binita helped him notice his shoulders and breathe out slowly, which relaxed his body so the words came out clearly.

qa.q: How might Binita see her brother's whisper of “Shoulders” the next morning?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and protective, seeing that he remembered the trick and trusted her to help. 😊

grounding: A child's tight shoulders before asking in class show nervousness, and a sibling's breathing trick helps.

passage:
Teacher's note from Vikas, Class UKG, Monday

Today was Charu's turn for show-and-tell. When I called her name, her shoulders crept right up to her ears and stayed there. She held her seashell against her chest and didn't move.

I knelt down and said, "Let's take two slow breaths together." We breathed. Her shoulders dropped a little. I gave her a small nod from my chair.

"This is my shell from the beach," she said, very softly. The class clapped. She smiled all afternoon. 🙂

qa.q: What did Charu hold against her chest?
qa.a: Her seashell.

qa.q: What was Charu probably feeling when her shoulders crept up to her ears?
qa.a: She was most likely nervous about speaking in front of the class. Holding the shell tight suggests she also wanted something safe to hold on to.

qa.q: Which choices helped Charu speak?
qa.a: Kneeling for two slow breaths together and then a small nod from the teacher's chair helped her shoulders relax enough to start. 😊

qa.q: How do the classmates respond when Charu speaks?
qa.a: They clap, which likely helps her feel proud, since she smiles all afternoon.

grounding: It shows a child holding her shoulders tight before speaking in class and slow breaths and a friendly nod easing her.
